entities.name: Stephen Kontostephanos
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Stephen Kontostephanos (died 1149) was a prominent Byzantine aristocrat and military commander whose career was deeply intertwined with the Komnenian restoration, serving under Emperor John II Komnenos and his son Manuel I Komnenos. His marriage to Anna Komnene, a daughter of Andronikos Komnenos and niece of Emperor Manuel I, solidified his position within the imperial family, reflecting the Komnenoi's strategy of consolidating power through marital alliances with loyal aristocratic houses. His military exploits, particularly in the Balkans and against the Normans, were crucial in defending and expanding the Byzantine Empire's influence during a period of intense geopolitical competition in the 12th century.

Kontostephanos distinguished himself in several key campaigns. He played a significant role in John II's campaigns against the Serbs and Hungarians in the 1130s, helping to reassert Byzantine suzerainty in the Balkans. His most notable military action, however, came during the reign of Manuel I. In 1149, as *megas doux* (Grand Duke) of the Byzantine fleet, he led a major naval expedition against the Norman Kingdom of Sicily, aiming to recover Corfu. During the protracted siege of Corfu, Kontostephanos was struck by an arrow and died, a considerable blow to the Byzantine war effort and a personal loss for Emperor Manuel, who held him in high regard.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Stephen Kontostephanos was a significant military figure whose death during the Siege of Corfu in 1149 represented a tactical setback for Emperor Manuel I Komnenos's ambitious Western policies. His career highlights the importance of military aristocrats and strategic marriages in the Komnenian restoration of the Byzantine Empire.
